lead: A matrix converter is a direct AC-to-AC converter. Nine bidirectional switches connect three input phases to three output phases. By closing the right switches for the right times, it makes an output of chosen voltage and frequency. There is no rectifier, no DC link and no large capacitor. The same switches carry current in both directions, so power can flow back to the supply. Compact motor drives, wind turbines and aircraft supplies use it where size and reliability matter.
prereq: You need: Unit 1 for bidirectional switches, Chapter 5.4 for PWM chopping, and Chapter 5.5 for building a new frequency by switching.

blocks.text: A matrix converter connects three input phases a, b, c to three output phases A, B, C through nine switches. The nine switches are numbered row by row. S<sub>1</sub>, S<sub>2</sub>, S<sub>3</sub> connect inputs a, b, c to output A; S<sub>4</sub>, S<sub>5</sub>, S<sub>6</sub> connect a, b, c to output B; S<sub>7</sub>, S<sub>8</sub>, S<sub>9</sub> connect a, b, c to output C. Every switch is bidirectional: it carries current and blocks voltage in both directions. A common build is two IGBTs with series diodes, connected in antiparallel. The switch array replaces the rectifier, DC link and inverter of a back-to-back drive.

Two rules keep the circuit safe. First, never close two switches in the same output row. If S1 and S2 close together, input phases a and b meet at output A: a line-to-line short. Second, never leave an output row with all three switches open. An inductive load current must have a path; breaking it causes a voltage spike. Most modulation therefore keeps exactly one switch closed in each output row. In many states two or three outputs share one input phase. The zero states connect all three outputs to a single input. The mix of states chosen sets the input current waveform and its balance.

Each output row has three choices, so 3³ = 27 switch states are possible. The figure shows one state: S2, S6 and S7 closed, so A gets b, B gets c and C gets a. Over a switching period the controller moves through states so the average output follows the wanted sine.

Let T<sub>s</sub> be the switching period, chosen much shorter than the output period. Let d<sub>Aa</sub>, d<sub>Ab</sub>, d<sub>Ac</sub> be the fractions of T<sub>s</sub> for which output A is connected to inputs a, b, c. For output A, d<sub>Aa</sub> + d<sub>Ab</sub> + d<sub>Ac</sub> = 1. The average output phase voltage over one switching period is v<sub>A</sub> = d<sub>Aa</sub>v<sub>a</sub> + d<sub>Ab</sub>v<sub>b</sub> + d<sub>Ac</sub>v<sub>c</sub>. Here v<sub>a</sub>, v<sub>b</sub>, v<sub>c</sub> are the instantaneous input phase voltages. Similar equations hold for outputs B and C.

The scalar or Venturini method solves for duty cycles that make v<sub>A</sub>, v<sub>B</sub>, v<sub>C</sub> sinusoids at the wanted output frequency ω<sub>o</sub>. Space-vector modulation does the same with vectors and a switching table. In both, the output average is a weighted average of the three input voltages at that instant.

Let V<sub>in</sub> be the input phase RMS voltage and V<sub>o</sub> the output phase RMS voltage. The voltage transfer ratio is q = V<sub>o</sub> / V<sub>in</sub>. In the linear range q ≤ √3/2 ≈ 0.866. The limit comes from the envelope of the three input phase voltages. At any instant the output must lie between the largest and the smallest of v<sub>a</sub>, v<sub>b</sub>, v<sub>c</sub>. That envelope has peak V<sub>in,peak</sub> and its lowest peak is V<sub>in,peak</sub> × cos 30° = (√3/2)V<sub>in,peak</sub>, so the biggest clean sine output has peak (√3/2) times the input peak. Here V<sub>in,peak</sub> = √2 V<sub>in</sub> is the peak input phase voltage. A request for q = 1 forces duty cycles outside the valid range; the output clips and distorts.
The input current is chopped by the switches. A small LC input filter smooths it. The filter also removes the high-frequency components that would otherwise pollute the supply.

Bidirectional switches cannot change over instantly. If one switch opens before the next closes, the load current is interrupted. If both close, the supply is shorted. Four-step current-direction commutation solves this. The controller senses or estimates the current direction, then uses a short sequence of make-before-break steps that always leaves a safe path. The cost is extra switching logic.

Power can flow from supply to load or from load to supply. The switches are bidirectional and there is no diode rectifier to block reverse power. A motor can brake and return energy to the line. This natural regeneration is useful in lifts, cranes and wind turbines.

There is no DC-link capacitor. That removes a bulky, life-limited component and gives a compact converter. The price is a maximum voltage gain of 0.866, more complex control and an input filter that must be designed for the chopped current.

Compare a back-to-back inverter: rectifier, DC-link capacitor, inverter. It is simpler and can use standard motor control, but the capacitor is large and regeneration needs an active front end. A matrix converter is direct, bidirectional and compact. It suits integrated motor drives, wind power and aerospace supplies where weight and reliability matter.

figure.caption: One valid switch state: S2 connects input b to output A, S6 connects c to B, and S7 connects a to C. Each output row has exactly one closed switch; this state also uses each input once.

spec.title: 3×3 switch matrix
spec.aria: A three-by-three table of switches S1 to S9, one row per output phase and one column per input phase, with one closed switch marked in each output row and no two in the same column.

examples.question: A 415 V, 50 Hz three-phase supply feeds a star-connected load of R = 20 Ω per phase through a three-phase matrix converter. The voltage transfer ratio is q = 0.5 and the output frequency is 30 Hz. Find the output phase voltage, output current and total power. Check whether the design is valid.
steps: Output phase voltage: V<sub>o</sub> = q × V<sub>ph,in</sub> = 0.5 × 239.6 = 119.8 V.
Output current per phase: I = V<sub>o</sub> / R = 119.8 / 20 = 5.99 A.
Power per phase: P<sub>ph</sub> = V<sub>o</sub>² / R = 119.8² / 20 = 717.6 W.
Total power: P = 3 × P<sub>ph</sub> = 3 × 717.6 = 2152.8 W = 2.15 kW.
Design check: q = 0.5 is below the linear limit 0.866, so the modulation is valid. The 30 Hz output is set by switching, not by the 50 Hz input.
examples.answer: V<sub>o</sub> = 119.8 V per phase, I = 5.99 A, P = 2.15 kW; q = 0.5 is below 0.866, so the design is valid.
examples.check:
import math
V_line = 415.0
R = 20.0
q = 0.5
V_ph_in = V_line / math.sqrt(3)
V_o = q * V_ph_in
I = V_o / R
P_kW = 3 * V_o**2 / R / 1000
print(f"{V_ph_in:.1f}")
print(f"{V_o:.1f}")
print(f"{I:.2f}")
print(f"{P_kW:.2f}")

traps: Do not close two switches in the same output row. That connects two input phases to one output and short-circuits the supply. If a diagram looks rotated, identify rows and columns first.
Do not expect q = 1. Linear modulation stops at 0.866; above that the output is not a clean sine.
No DC-link capacitor does not mean no stored energy. The input filter and the load inductance store energy, and the filter still needs design.
Never leave an output leg open with an inductive load; the current path must be continuous.
The voltage transfer ratio q is an output-to-input phase voltage ratio. It is not a transformer turns ratio and it does not set the output frequency; the switching does.

quiz.q: How many bidirectional switches does a three-phase to three-phase matrix converter use?
quiz.a: Nine switches, arranged in a 3×3 array.

quiz.q: Why is there no DC-link capacitor in a matrix converter?
quiz.a: It converts AC to AC directly. The switches connect input phases to output phases, so there is no intermediate DC stage and no large DC energy buffer. The input filter is small and is not a DC link.

quiz.q: A 400 V line-to-line, 50 Hz supply feeds a matrix converter with q = 0.7. Find the output phase voltage. Is q valid?
quiz.a: V<sub>ph,in</sub> = 400 / √3 = 230.9 V. V<sub>o</sub> = 0.7 × 230.9 = 161.7 V. q = 0.7 is below 0.866, so it is valid.

quiz.q: The controller closes S1 and S2 together. Explain the fault.
quiz.a: S1 connects input a to output A. S2 connects input b to output A. Both input phases a and b are shorted through output A, causing a large current and likely device damage.

quiz.q: Why is four-step commutation needed in a matrix converter?
quiz.a: The switches are bidirectional and the load current direction is not fixed. Opening all switches in an output leg interrupts inductive current and causes overvoltage. Closing the wrong switch shorts the supply. Four-step commutation uses current direction to make before break through safe intermediate states.

quiz.q: Compare a matrix converter with a back-to-back inverter for a regenerative motor drive.
quiz.a: A matrix converter is direct, has no DC-link capacitor, is compact and regenerates naturally through bidirectional switches. Its limits are q ≤ 0.866 and complex commutation. A back-to-back inverter is simpler and uses standard controls, but the DC-link capacitor is bulky and regeneration needs an active front end.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of the input filter in a matrix converter?
quiz.a: It smooths the chopped input current and reduces high-frequency harmonics injected into the supply.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry is moving to SiC and GaN bidirectional switches to cut losses and raise switching frequency. Sparse matrix converters use fewer switches. Multilevel matrix converters target higher voltage. Researchers work on commutation without current sensors and on grid-forming control for wind. Search terms: direct AC-AC converter, Venturini modulation, four-step commutation, sparse matrix converter.
